title: Documentation and README Practices
learningObjectives: Document setup, run, and test steps
Keep instructions current with code changes
Link to deeper documentation rather than duplicating it

understand.concept: A README is a front door to a repository: it should tell a reader what the project is, how to set it up, run it, test it, and where to find important information. Documentation should be accurate, concise, maintained with the code, and suited to its audience. Avoid assuming undocumented knowledge.
understand.whyItMatters: Documentation, reproducible setup, release clarity, and responsible reuse help collaborators and users work with software confidently.
understand.analogy: A well-labeled kit includes a description, instructions, version information, and notes about borrowed components.
understand.analogyLimit: Software has evolving dependencies, platform-specific behavior, and license terms that a physical kit analogy cannot fully express.

explain.narrative:
A README is a front door to a repository: it should tell a reader what the project is, how to set it up, run it, test it, and where to find important information. Documentation should be accurate, concise, maintained with the code, and suited to its audience. Avoid assuming undocumented knowledge.

Prefer concise, accurate information that a new contributor can follow. Verify instructions and sources when they change, and record any important limitations or conditions.

examples.explanation: A short project name gives readers a starting point.

examples.title: Document repeatable commands
examples.explanation: Ordered commands make setup and verification easier to follow.

examples.title: Capture version context
examples.explanation: Recording a version can help compare environments or releases.

examples.title: Summarize a change
examples.explanation: A concise change summary helps readers understand what changed.

examples.title: Track an external source
examples.explanation: Recording source and license status supports responsible reuse.

commonMistakes: Assuming versions or operating systems behave identically
Publishing changes without a clear summary
Treating third-party material as unrestricted because it is publicly visible
Failing to record important limitations or required notices
